text: For my Master's thesis I want to do something about ML monitoring. At my student job our churn model quietly got worse for months before anyone noticed — is there a thesis in that?

There's likely a thesis in this, but the interesting part isn't "the
model got worse" — it's *why nobody noticed*. That's actually two
different failure modes wearing the same costume.

When your churn model degraded, was it that the *predictions* silently
drifted — or that nobody could even *check* accuracy, because you only
find out if someone actually churned weeks or months later?

Honestly both, but mostly the second — churn labels only arrive weeks later. Our dashboard alerted so often that everyone ignored it, and nobody could say whether a high score actually meant the model was worse.

So the "detect drift without labels" problem and the "stop crying
wolf" problem are both already being worked on separately. What none of
these seem to do is close the loop back to what actually happened weeks
later — whether the drift alerts *would have* predicted the real
accuracy drop once the labels finally arrived.
Before writing anything: can you find proper literature for this? Real papers only — I've heard too many stories about made-up citations.

Literature base is now 15 references, all individually verified against
Crossref or arXiv — DOIs resolved and titles cross-checked. Among them:

  - Sethi & Kantardzic — MD3, an unsupervised drift detector built
    to cut false alarms (the alert-fatigue problem)
  - Zhang, Bui & Apley (2023) — score-vector monitoring, an
    alternative signal to compare against drift metrics

Keyword searches that mostly returned noise — IoT intrusion detection,
materials-science "fatigue" papers — were rejected rather than
force-fit.
